sketches.title: Gourd of Honor
sketches.premise: The Host announces a very ordinary vegetable, and both players give it a grand ceremonial slogan. Make the vegetable sound worthy of a parade, medal, or national anthem without losing what it is.
sketches.criterion: The slogan must still make the named vegetable recognizable as a vegetable, with its real identity and edible role intact.
sketches.move_shape: Write one slogan under 90 characters; for a carrot: “Carrot: The orange root that marches bravely into every lunch.”
sketches.first_card: A carrot is an orange root vegetable.

sketches.title: The Vegetable Case
sketches.premise: A vegetable stands before the court, accused of being boring. Both players deliver a slogan that builds its case, using the vegetable’s plain facts as evidence. The strongest defense turns humble details into a stirring cause.
sketches.criterion: The slogan must keep the card’s stated fact about the vegetable true while presenting it as a reason to admire that vegetable.
sketches.move_shape: Write one slogan under 90 characters; for peas: “Peas: Tiny green proof that good things travel in groups.”
sketches.first_card: Peas are small, round, green seeds that grow in pods.

sketches.title: Harvest Broadcast
sketches.premise: The Host is reporting live from the world of vegetables. Both players write a slogan that makes one quiet vegetable fact sound like urgent public news, while the fact remains on the record.
sketches.criterion: The slogan must preserve the card’s checkable vegetable fact, even if its importance, cause, or consequences are wildly enlarged.
sketches.move_shape: Write one broadcast-style slogan under 90 characters; for a potato: “Potato underground network expands beneath dinner tables.”

sketches.title: Garden Medal
sketches.premise: Each card names a vegetable and a plain achievement, such as growing in a pod or having edible leaves. Both players award that vegetable a medal with a slogan that turns the achievement into glory. The Host checks whether the medal still belongs to the right vegetable for the right reason.
sketches.criterion: The slogan must keep both named parts true: the vegetable and the card’s stated achievement or trait.
sketches.move_shape: Write a medal inscription or slogan under 90 characters; for spinach: “Spinach, honored for leaves that make every salad look prepared.”

sketches.title: The Crisp Ceremony
sketches.premise: The Host presents a vegetable at a grand ceremony and asks for its official motto. Both players may invent titles, traditions, and dramatic promises, but the vegetable must still fit the card’s two ordinary facts. The joke is in the ceremony, not at the expense of the player.
sketches.criterion: The motto must keep the card’s two facts about the vegetable in shape, without replacing either one with a different vegetable or feature.
sketches.move_shape: Write an official motto under 90 characters; for corn: “Corn: Tall in the field, golden on the plate, punctual at harvest.”
sketches.first_card: Corn grows on tall stalks and has yellow kernels.

sketches.title: Market of Marvels
sketches.premise: A market stall gives each vegetable a slogan meant to win a ribbon from a very serious judge. Both players can sell wonder, usefulness, or heroic promise, but the slogan must honestly carry the card’s two everyday details. The more imaginative the sales pitch, the better—if the details survive.
sketches.criterion: The slogan must retain both named facts, so a reader can still accept them as true from the slogan alone.
sketches.move_shape: Write a market slogan under 90 characters; for cucumber: “Cucumber: Long, green, and ready to bring a cool streak to lunch.”
sketches.first_card: A cucumber is long and green.
